## 2.1 Heterozygosity                 
```{r}
# read in Heterozygosity data calculted using vcftools
hetstats <- read.table("Final.SLF.het", header=T)
popdata <- read.csv("2022 SLF Info new.csv", header=T) 
#population list in same order as bed file, ordered by SLF ID

#Observed heterozygosity (O.HET) is calculated as the total number of sites (N_SITES) minus the number of homozygous sites (O.HOM).
hetstats$O.HET <- hetstats$N_SITES - hetstats$O.HOM.

#Expected heterozygosity (E.HET) is similarly calculated as the total number of sites minus the expected number of homozygous sites (E.HOM).
hetstats$E.HET <- hetstats$N_SITES - hetstats$E.HOM.

#measure of the proportion of observed heterozygous sites in each individual.
hetstats$Ho <- hetstats$O.HET/hetstats$N_SITES

#measure of the proportion of expected heterozygous sites in each individual.
hetstats$He <- hetstats$E.HET/hetstats$N_SITES

#merge with population data
hetstats <- merge(hetstats, popdata, by.x="INDV", by.y="fly_ID")
head(hetstats)

#Since O.HET can never be greater than N_SITES (an individual cannot have more heterozygous sites than the total number of genotyped sites), the ratio O.HET/N_SITES will always be between 0 and 1.

# Calculate the mean and standard deviation of observed heterozygosity (Ho)
mean_Ho <- mean(hetstats$Ho, na.rm = TRUE)
sd_Ho <- sd(hetstats$Ho, na.rm = TRUE)

# Calculate the mean and standard deviation of expected heterozygosity (He)
mean_He <- mean(hetstats$He, na.rm = TRUE)
sd_He <- sd(hetstats$He, na.rm = TRUE)

# Calculate the mean and standard deviation of inbreeding coefficient F(HOM)
mean_F <- mean(hetstats$F, na.rm = TRUE)
sd_F <- sd(hetstats$F, na.rm = TRUE)

# Sample size (excluding NA values)
n_He <- sum(!is.na(hetstats$He))
n_Ho <- sum(!is.na(hetstats$Ho))
n_F <- sum(!is.na(hetstats$F))

# Calculate confidence intervals (95%)
ci_He <- qt(0.975, df = n_He - 1) * sd_He / sqrt(n_He)
ci_Ho <- qt(0.975, df = n_Ho - 1) * sd_Ho / sqrt(n_Ho)
ci_F <- qt(0.975, df = n_F - 1) * sd_F / sqrt(n_F)


```

## 2.3 Calculate the Ne (effetive population size for momi2 later)
```{r}
# Keightley, P. D., Ness, R. W., Halligan, D. L., & Haddrill, P. R. (2014). Estimation of the spontaneous mutation rate per nucleotide site in a Drosophila melanogaster full-sib family. Genetics, 196(1), 313–320. https://doi.org/10.1534/genetics.113.158758

#"For Drosophila melanogaster there are relatively few estimates, ranging from 2.8 × 10−9 to 6.0 × 10−9 site−1 gen−1 (Haag-Liautard et al. 2007; Keightley et al. 2009, 2014; Schrider et al."
mu <- 2.8e-9

# Calculate average observed heterozygosity (Ho) across all individuals
average_Ho <- mean(hetstats$Ho)

# Calculate average expected heterozygosity (He) across all individuals
average_He <- mean(hetstats$He)

# You can use either average_Ho or average_He as your H for the Ne calculation
# Here, I'll use average_He
H <- average_He

# Calculate Ne using the formula
Ne <- H / (4 * mu * (1 - H))

# Print the estimated Ne
print(paste("Estimated effective population size (Ne) is:", Ne))

```

##2.4 Runs of homozygosity using plink, Figure 2A.
--homozyg-density 30 --homozyg-gap 1000 --homozyg-kb 500 --homozyg-snp 50 --homozyg-window-het 1 --homozyg-window-snp 30 --homozyg-window-missing 5 --homozyg-window-threshold 0.05
The -homozyg option in PLINK v1.9 makes ROH calls using a sliding window that scans along an individual's SNP data to detect homozygous stretches. PLINK first determines whether a given SNP is potentially in a ROH. To call a SNP as part of a ROH, PLINK calculates the proportion of completely homozygous windows that encompass that SNP. For example, a SNP inside a 100 SNP window has 100 chances to be part of a homozygous stretch as the window slides across one SNP at a time. Using the default -homozyg-window-threshold of 0.05, if 5% of these windows are completely homozygous, then the SNP will be included in the ROH. Finally, a ROH is called if the number of such "ROH SNPs" in a row surpasses a user-defined threshold in terms of SNPs (default = 100) and/or kb distance (default = 1, 000). PLINK provides numerous other user-defined parameters, such as the size of the sliding window measured in units of SNP length (default = 50), the number of heterozygous SNPs (default = 1) allowed in the ROH, the number of missing SNPs (default = 5) allowed in the ROH, and several other parameters detailed on the PLINK website (see http://pngu.mgh.harvard.edu/~purcell/plink/ 

```{r}
# Load necessary libraries
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)

# Read the PLINK RoH data
plink_roh <- read.delim('/Users/fallonmong/Documents/Documents - Fallon MacBook Pro/FallonPaper Final/Final/RoHPlink/SLF_data.hom', sep = '')

# Re-categorize ROH segments into size classes
plink_roh_size <- plink_roh %>%
  mutate(size_class = case_when(
    KB >= 500 & KB < 1000 ~ "0.5-1 Mb",
    KB >= 1000 & KB < 5000 ~ "1-5 Mb",
    KB >= 5000 ~ ">5 Mb"
  ))

# Recount the number of ROH segments and calculate total length in each size class for each sample
plink_roh_size_counts <- plink_roh_size %>%
  group_by(FID, size_class) %>%
  summarise(roh_count = n(), total_length = sum(KB), .groups = 'drop')

# Merge with location data
plink_roh_size_counts <- plink_roh_size_counts %>%
  left_join(popdata, by = c("FID" = "fly_ID"))

# Order the samples by area
plink_roh_size_counts <- plink_roh_size_counts %>%
  arrange(area, FID) %>%
  mutate(FID = factor(FID, levels = unique(FID)))

# Calculate the average number of RoH segments per size class and area, adjusted for sample size
plink_area_size_counts <- plink_roh_size_counts %>%
  group_by(area, size_class) %>%
  summarise(total_roh_count = sum(roh_count),
            sample_size = n_distinct(FID),
            avg_roh_count = total_roh_count / sample_size, .groups = 'drop')

# Calculate the total number of ROH per area
total_roh_per_area <- plink_roh_size_counts %>%
  group_by(area) %>%
  summarise(
    total_roh_count = sum(roh_count),
    sample_size = n_distinct(FID)
  ) %>%
  mutate(avg_roh_count = total_roh_count / sample_size)


# Define colors for size classes
size_class_colors <- c("0.5-1 Mb" = "#009E73", "1-5 Mb" = "#e6ab02", ">5 Mb" = "#c861a5")

# order the size
plink_area_size_counts <- plink_area_size_counts %>%
  mutate(size_class = factor(size_class, levels = c("0.5-1 Mb", "1-5 Mb", ">5 Mb")))

# Average number of RoH segments by size class and area (side-by-side)
Roh_count <- ggplot(plink_area_size_counts, aes(x = area, y = avg_roh_count, fill = size_class)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = position_dodge()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = size_class_colors) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) + 
  labs(x = NULL,
       y = "Total number of ROHs",
       fill = "Size Class") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        axis.title.y = element_text(size = 15),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12))

# Save the plot. Figure 2A.
ggsave("number_ROH.png", Roh_count, dpi = 300)
ggsave("number_ROH.pdf", Roh_count)

```
```{r}
#calculate the FROH
# Genomic inbreeding coefficients were determined utilizing PLINK. The calculation method of FROH was as follows: FROH = (LROH/LAUTO) [38], where LROH represents the sum length of an individual’s ROH in the genome, and LAUTO is the specific length of the autosomal genome covered by SNPs of SLF (2252044789 bp).

# 1: Calculate the number of ROH segments for each sample
plink_roh_counts <- plink_roh %>%
  group_by(FID) %>%
  summarise(roh_count = n())

# 2: Calculate the total length of ROH segments for each sample
plink_roh_lengths <- plink_roh %>%
  group_by(FID) %>%
  summarise(total_length = sum(KB))

# Combine the counts and lengths into one dataframe
plink_roh_summary <- plink_roh_counts %>%
  inner_join(plink_roh_lengths, by = "FID")

# Merge with location data
plink_roh_summary <- plink_roh_summary %>%
  left_join(popdata, by = c("FID" = "fly_ID"))

# Order the samples by area
plink_roh_summary <- plink_roh_summary %>%
  mutate(FID = factor(FID, levels = unique(FID[order(area)])))

# Define the genome length covered by SLF SNPs
LAUTO <- 2252044789/1000 #kb

# Calculate FROH for each individual
plink_roh_summary <- plink_roh_summary %>%
  mutate(FROH = total_length / LAUTO)

# FROH per area group
FROH <- ggplot(plink_roh_summary, aes(x = area, y = FROH, fill = area)) +
  geom_violin(aes(fill = area), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(color = area), alpha = 0.8, size = 3) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = location_colors) +
  scale_color_manual(values = location_colors) +
  labs(x = NULL,
       y = "F(ROH)") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        axis.title.y = element_text(size = 14),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 14))

# Save the plot. Figure 2C.
ggsave("FROH.png", FROH, dpi = 300)
ggsave("FROH.pdf", FROH)
```

```{r}
### Calcaulte some stats, save it as csv. Supplementary table S2.

# Calculate average FROH by area
plink_roh_summary_area <- plink_roh_summary %>%
  group_by(area) %>%
  summarise(mean_froh = mean(FROH))

#save it as csv
write.csv(plink_roh_summary_area, file = "plink_merged_summary_roh_segments.csv", row.names = FALSE)

mean_froh <- mean(plink_roh_summary$FROH)
se_froh <- sd(plink_roh_summary$FROH) / sqrt(nrow(plink_roh_summary))

# Calculate the 95% confidence interval
alpha <- 0.05
t_value <- qt(1 - alpha / 2, df = nrow(plink_roh_summary) - 1)
ci_lower <- mean_froh - t_value * se_froh
ci_upper <- mean_froh + t_value * se_froh

# Print the results
cat("Mean FROH:", mean_froh, "\n")
cat("Standard Error (SE):", se_froh, "\n")
cat("95% Confidence Interval (CI): [", ci_lower, ",", ci_upper, "]\n")

```


## 2.5 Tajima'D and Nucleotide Diversity
Nucleotide diversity (often referred to using the symbol π) is the average pairwise difference between all possible pairs of individuals in our sample. It is a very intuitive and simple measure of genetic diversity, and is accurately estimated even with very few samples. .
We can obtain the nucleotide diversity (π) from our VCF file using vcftools software. In our case we will collect the π value from each 10 kb (10,000 bp) window of the genome.

```{r}
# Load required libraries
library(ggplot2)

setwd("~/Documents/Documents - Fallon MacBook Pro/FallonPaper Final/Final/Pi")

# Read the data
Pi <- read.table("/Users/fallonmong/Documents/Documents - Fallon MacBook Pro/FallonPaper Final/Final/Final.SLF.PI.windowed.pi", header=TRUE)

TD <- read.table("Final.SLF.TajimaD", header=TRUE)

# Calculating the mean
print(paste("Mean of Tajima's D:", mean(TD$TajimaD, na.rm = TRUE)))
print(paste("Mean of Pi:", mean(Pi$PI)))

# Histogram of TajimaD. Figure 2D.
# 10KB window
pdf("Tajimas_D_10KB.pdf", width=8, height=6)
png("Tajimas_D_10KB.png")
hist(TD$Tajima, breaks=30, col="lightblue", xlab="Tajima's D", main="")
# Add a red vertical line at Tajima's D mean
abline(v=0.157, col="red", lwd=2)
# Close the PDF device

# Calculate the mean of Pi
mean_pi <- mean(Pi$PI)

# Create the plot across genome region

  theme_minimal() +

    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),

ggsave(filename="PI.pdf", PI_plot)
ggsave(filename="PI.png", plot=PI_plot, dpi = 300)

```

# Part 3: Population Structure.
## 3.1 DAPC
DAPC(Discriminant Analysis of Principal Components)
This multivariate approach allows for the exploration of genetic variation by constructing synthetic variables from linear combinations of alleles, where these variables are designed to capture the essence of genetic diversity among individuals. Run DAPC with adegenet, run the job below on hpc, it's memory demanding.Do not run in R markdown here.

```{r}
# Load required libraries
library(adegenet)
library(vcfR)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(tidyverse)
library(data.table)

# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(0314)

# Read the VCF file
vcf <- read.vcfR("/Users/fallonmong/Documents/Documents - Fallon MacBook Pro/FallonPaper Old/10KB.maf0.01.missing0.9.id0.2.vcf")

location_colors <- c("Bronx" = "#252525", 
                     "Brooklyn" =  "#e6ab02",
                     "Camden, NJ" = "#a65628",
                     "Connecticut" = "#e41a1c" ,
                     "Governor Island" = "#08589e",
                     "Manhattan" = "#c861a5",
                     "Staten island" = "#3690c0",
                     "West Orange, NJ" = "#009E73")

popdata <- read.csv("2022 SLF Info new.csv", header=T) 
#link populations
popgen_sort <- popdata[order(popdata$fly_ID),c("fly_ID","area")] 
#ordered and reduced to just columns we need

# Convert VCF to genlight object
slf.gen = vcfR2genlight(vcf)

#assigns the 'area' column of the sorted dataframe to the 'pop' slot of the genlight object.
pop(slf.gen) <- popgen_sort[,2] #assign populations to gen file
slf.gen@pop #verify population attribute

#find cluster
clusters_result <- find.clusters(slf.gen,parallel = require("parallel"), n.cores=8)

SLF_dapc <- dapc(slf.gen, clusters_result$grp)

scatter(SLF_dapc, posi.da="bottomleft")

# cross-validation for the DAPC 
optx_slf <- xvalDapc(tab(slf.gen, NA.method = "mean"), pop(slf.gen), parallel="multicore", ncpus=8L)  
#look for leveling off window
optx_slf[2:7]

# Run DAPC after cross-validation and visualize DAPC, run it on hpc.

# In our data, DAPC suggests to supported retaining 35 principal component axes to achieve the lowest MSE and 7 discriminant functions that captured 53.4% of the genetic variation. 

dapc.allsamples35 <- dapc(slf.gen,  n.pca=35, n.da=7, var.contrib=T, scale=F,parallel = require("parallel"), n.cores=12)

#visualize DAPC
# Set up a PDF device
pdf("withlabel.SLF.PC35.da7.allsamples.png")
# Plot the DAPC scatter plot
scatter(dapc.allsamples35, clabel=0.9, col=location_colors,
        scree.pca=FALSE, scree.da =FALSE, cell=1.5, cex=1, mstree=FALSE)  # retain 2 df
# Turn off the device
dev.off() # Figure 3A

```

## 3.2 SNP-based phylogenetic tree
Tree built part was done on hpc scripts
```{r}
library(ape)
# Read the sample meta dataset
popdata <- read.csv("2022 SLF Info new.csv", header = TRUE) 

# Convert 'area' to a factor
popdata$area <- as.factor(popdata$area)

location_colors <- c("Bronx" = "#252525", 
                     "Brooklyn" =  "#e6ab02",
                     "Camden, NJ" = "#a65628",
                     "Connecticut" = "#e41a1c" ,
                     "Governor Island" = "#08589e",
                     "Manhattan" = "#c861a5",
                     "Staten island" = "#3690c0",
                     "West Orange, NJ" = "#009E73")

# Read the tree file
treefile <- read.tree("Final.SNPTree.treefile")

# Ensure the tree tip labels match with IDs in popdata
treefile$tip.label <- as.character(popdata$fly_ID)

# Map each tip label to its area based on popdata
tip_areas <- popdata$area[match(treefile$tip.label, popdata$fly_ID)]

# Replace tip labels with area names
treefile$tip.label <- as.character(tip_areas)

# Match the areas to the colors defined in location_colors
tip_colors <- location_colors[as.character(tip_areas)]

png("phylogenetic_tree_plot.pdf")
# Plot the fan tree with tip colors and area names as tip labels
ape::plot.phylo(x = treefile, type = "fan", tip.color = tip_colors)
# Close the PDF device
dev.off()
# Figure 3C
```
## 3.3 Admixture
K 1-10, 10 replicates each K for ADMIXTURE was done by hpc
```{r}
# Choose the best K
#Use ADMIXTURE’s cross-validation procedure. A good value of K will exhibit a low cross-validation error compared to other K values. 
setwd("/scratch/fm2371/Winchell/SLF_spring23/SLF_spring23/raw.vcf/Final/Admixture")

# Read in the data
data <- list.files(pattern = "Final\\.log.*\\.out", full.names = TRUE)

# Use lapply to read in all log files at once
bigData <- lapply(data, readLines)

# Find the line that starts with "CV error"
library(stringr)
foundset_cv <- sapply(bigData, function(x) x[which(str_detect(x, "^CV error"))])

# Extract the numeric value from the "CV error" line
cv_errors <- as.numeric(sub("CV error \\(K=\\d+\\): (-?\\d+\\.\\d+).*", "\\1", foundset_cv))

# Create a data frame with K values and corresponding CV errors
cv_df <- data.frame(
  K = rep(1:10, each = 10),
  cv_error = cv_errors
)

# Calculate the mean CV error for each K
cv_summary <- aggregate(cv_error ~ K, data = cv_df, FUN = mean)

cv_summary_plot <- ggplot(cv_summary, aes(x = K, y = cv_error)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2C3E50", size = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#E74C3C", size = 3) +
  #geom_text(aes(label = K), nudge_x = 0.2, nudge_y = 0.002, size = 4, color = "#2C3E50") +
  labs(x = "K", y = "Mean CV Error") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "gray90"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    plot.margin = unit(c(1, 1, 1, 1), "cm")
  ) +
  ggtitle("Mean CV Error over 10 replicates") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, max(cv_summary$K), by = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(min(cv_summary$cv_error) - 0.005, max(cv_summary$cv_error) + 0.005))

# Save the plot. Supplementary Figure S3.C
ggsave(filename="cv_summary_plot.pdf", plot=cv_summary_plot, width=12, height=8, units="in")
ggsave(filename="cv_summary_plot.png", plot=cv_summary_plot,dpi = 300)
```

# Part 4: Stats for momi2.
Calculate the average AIC serial stats and CI/Sd after 1100 bootstraps, find the best model of fit.
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# Step 1: Read and Clean Data
momi2_bt <- read_lines("best_model_params.txt") # Read the data from the text file

# Parse the data into a data frame
bootstrap_data <- data.frame(bootstrap = numeric(), parameter = character(), value = numeric(), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
current_bootstrap <- NA

for (line in momi2_bt) {
  if (grepl("Replicate", line)) {
    current_bootstrap <- as.numeric(gsub("\\D", "", line)) # Extract bootstrap number
  } else if (line != "") {
    parts <- strsplit(line, ": ")[[1]]
    # Ensure the value is read as numeric without rounding
    bootstrap_data <- rbind(bootstrap_data, data.frame(bootstrap = current_bootstrap, parameter = parts[1], value = as.numeric(parts[2], digits = 22)))
  }
}

# Reorder and rename the bootstrap_data, per 14 rows belongs to one bootstrap
n_rows_per_bootstrap <- 14
total_bootstraps <- floor(nrow(bootstrap_data) / n_rows_per_bootstrap)

# Remove any incomplete bootstrap sets
bootstrap_data <- bootstrap_data[1:(total_bootstraps * n_rows_per_bootstrap), ]

# Overwrite the 'bootstrap' column with the new sequence
bootstrap_data$bootstrap <- rep(1:total_bootstraps, each = n_rows_per_bootstrap)

# Step 2: Data Transformation
# Pivot the data for analysis
long_data_bt <- pivot_wider(
  bootstrap_data, 
  id_cols = bootstrap,  # Keep the bootstrap identifier
  names_from = parameter, 
  values_from = value
)

long_data_bt <- long_data_bt[, -c(16:23)]

# Step 3: Statistical Summary
# Calculate the mean, standard deviation, and 95% confidence intervals for each parameter
summary_stats <- long_data_bt %>%
  select(-bootstrap) %>% # Exclude the bootstrap column from summarisation
  unnest(cols = everything()) %>% # Unnest all list-columns
  summarise(across(everything(), list(
    mean = ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = ~ sd(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
    lower = ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE) - qt(0.975, df = length(.x) - 1) * sd(.x, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(length(.x)),
    upper = ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE) + qt(0.975, df = length(.x) - 1) * sd(.x, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(length(.x))
  ), .names = "{.col}_{.fn}")) # Custom naming to ensure correct splitting later


# Ensure the calculated statistics maintain their precision
summary_stats <- round(summary_stats, digits = 22)

# The rest of the code for creating plot_data and writing the stats remains the same

# Calculate the number of parameters (each parameter has mean, sd, lower, and upper statistics)
# Number of unique parameters, assuming each has 4 statistics (mean, sd, lower, upper)
num_parameters <- length(summary_stats) / 4

# Generate the parameter names by removing statistic suffixes and ensuring uniqueness
parameter_names <- unique(sub("_mean$|_sd$|_lower$|_upper$", "", names(summary_stats)))

# Verifying the corrected parameter names
parameter_names

# Ensure the length of 'parameter' and 'statistic' vectors match the length of 'value' vector
plot_data <- tibble(
  parameter = rep(parameter_names, each = 4),
  statistic = rep(c("Mean", "SD", "95% CI Lower", "95% CI Upper"), times = num_parameters),
  value = as.vector(t(summary_stats))
)

# Save all stats result. Supplementary Table. Table S1.
write.csv(plot_data, "stats.momi2.txt", sep = "\t", row.names = FALSE, quote = FALSE)

plot_data_wide <- plot_data %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = statistic, values_from = value)

write.csv(plot_data_wide, "stats.momi2.wide.csv", sep = "\t", row.names = FALSE, quote = FALSE)
```

Calculate the mean of all AIC stats over 1100 replicates
```{r}
# Load necessary library
library(stringr)

# Function to extract values from a line based on the pattern
extract_value <- function(line, pattern) {
  matches <- str_match(line, pattern)
  as.numeric(matches[1,2])
}

# Initialize lists to store values for each model
values <- list("Constant" = list(AIC = numeric(), Delta_AIC = numeric(), AIC_Weight = numeric()),
               "Expansion" = list(AIC = numeric(), Delta_AIC = numeric(), AIC_Weight = numeric()),
               "Decline" = list(AIC = numeric(), Delta_AIC = numeric(), AIC_Weight = numeric()),
               "Decline and Expand" = list(AIC = numeric(), Delta_AIC = numeric(), AIC_Weight = numeric()),
               "Complex US" = list(AIC = numeric(), Delta_AIC = numeric(), AIC_Weight = numeric()),
               "Complex Global" = list(AIC = numeric(), Delta_AIC = numeric(), AIC_Weight = numeric()))

# Read the file line by line
lines <- readLines("aic_and_likelihoods.txt")

# Loop over each line
for (line in lines) {
  # Check if the line contains the information and process it
  if (grepl("AIC:", line)) {
    # Determine which model the line refers to and extract values
    for (model in names(values)) {
      if (grepl(model, line)) {
        values[[model]]$AIC <- c(values[[model]]$AIC, extract_value(line, "AIC: ([0-9.]+)"))
        values[[model]]$Delta_AIC <- c(values[[model]]$Delta_AIC, extract_value(line, "Delta AIC: ([0-9.]+)"))
        values[[model]]$AIC_Weight <- c(values[[model]]$AIC_Weight, extract_value(line, "AIC Weight: ([0-9.e-]+)"))
      }
    }
  }
}

# Calculate mean values for each model and parameter
mean_values <- lapply(values, function(model_values) sapply(model_values, mean))

# Convert to a more structured format (dataframe) for saving
mean_values_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(mean_values), function(model) {
  cbind(Model = model, t(data.frame(mean_values[[model]])))
}))

# Ensure mean_values_df is a dataframe
mean_values_df <- data.frame(mean_values_df)

# Rename the levels of the Model factor
mean_values_df$Model <- factor(mean_values_df$Model, levels = c("Constant", "Expansion", "Decline", 
                                                                "Decline and Expand", "Complex US", "Complex Global"),
                               labels = c("Constant Model", "Expansion Model", "Decline Model", 
                                          "One Bottleneck Model", "Two Bottlenecks Model", "Three Bottlenecks Model"))


# Save the means to a CSV file. Main text table. Table 1.
write.csv(mean_values_df, "mean_model_values.csv", row.names = FALSE)

```


#Part 5: Landscape Genetics
## 5.1 IBD (Isolation By Distance)
Genetic distances were calculated as 1 minus the identity-by-state (IBS) values using PLINK v1.09 (Purcell et al., 2007), providing a measure of genetic divergence, with values closer to 1 indicating greater dissimilarity. This was done on hpc.

Isolation by geographic distance
```{r}
# 1. Isolation by geographic distance
library(hierfstat)
library(geodist)
library(ecodist)
library(adespatial)
library(vegan)
library(ggplot2)

# Read in geo data
xySLF <- read.delim("2022 SLF Pop Gen Data.txt")
names(xySLF) <- c("ID", "latitude", "longitude")
xySLF$ID <- paste0(xySLF$ID, "_a")

# Calculate the geographic distances using the Vincenty method and convert to kilometers
geographic_dist_matrix_km <- geodist(xySLF, measure = "Vincenty") / 1000

# Convert the geographic distance matrix to a dist object
geographic_dist_km <- as.dist(geographic_dist_matrix_km)

# Assuming geo_dist_matrix is a matrix with row and column names that match the IDs in xySLF$ID
geo_dist_matrix <- as.matrix(geographic_dist_matrix_km)
rownames(geographic_dist_matrix_km) <- xySLF$ID
colnames(geographic_dist_matrix_km) <- xySLF$ID

max_value <- max(geo_dist_matrix)
print(paste("Maximum geo distance:", max_value))

# Calculate the mean value of genetic distances
mean_value <- mean(geo_dist_matrix)
print(paste("Mean geo distance:", mean_value))
min(geo_dist_matrix)
max(geo_dist_matrix)

# Log-transform the geographic distance matrix
geo_dist_matrix_log <- log(geo_dist_matrix + 1)

# Change to long format
geo_dist_long <- reshape2::melt(geographic_dist_matrix_km)
names(geo_dist_long) <- c("ID1", "ID2", "GeoDistance")

# Load the genetic distance calculated by plink
# Convert the genetic distance matrix to a dist object
genetic_dist <- read.delim('Final.SLF.mdist', header = F)
genetic_dist <- as.matrix(genetic_dist)

max_value <- max(genetic_dist)
print(paste("Maximum genetic distance:", max_value))

# Calculate the mean value of genetic distances
mean_value <- mean(genetic_dist)
print(paste("Mean genetic distance:", mean_value))

# Set the column and row names of the matrix
colnames(genetic_dist) <- xySLF$ID
rownames(genetic_dist) <- xySLF$ID

# Change it to long format
ibs_long <- reshape2::melt(as.matrix(genetic_dist))
names(ibs_long) <- c("ID1", "ID2", "IBSDistance")

# Make sure they are character
geo_dist_long$ID1 <- as.character(geo_dist_long$ID1)
geo_dist_long$ID2 <- as.character(geo_dist_long$ID2)
ibs_long$ID1 <- as.character(ibs_long$ID1)
ibs_long$ID2 <- as.character(ibs_long$ID2)

# Merge the two datasets
combined_data_ibs <- merge(geo_dist_long, ibs_long, by = c("ID1", "ID2"))
combined_data_ibs <- combined_data_ibs[combined_data_ibs$GeoDistance > 0, ] # removing zero distances if any

# Log-transform the distances
combined_data_ibs$GeoDistance_log <- log(combined_data_ibs$GeoDistance + 1)
combined_data_ibs$IBSDistance_log <- log(combined_data_ibs$IBSDistance + 1)

IBS_dist_Geo_log <- ggplot(combined_data_ibs, aes(x = GeoDistance_log, y = IBSDistance)) +
  geom_point(color = "#3690c0") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "black") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),  # Remove grid lines
        axis.line = element_line(color = "black", size = 0.3)) +  # Add axis lines
  labs(x = "Log Geographic Pairwise Distance (km)", y = "Genetic Pairwise Distance")

#mentel test
mantel_result_log <- mantel(genetic_dist, geo_dist_matrix_log, method = "pearson", permutations = 9999)
print(mantel_result_log)

# Saving the plot. Figure 5A.
ggsave("Geo_IBS_log.pdf", plot = IBS_dist_Geo_log, width = 10, height = 8)
ggsave("Geo_IBS_log.png", plot = IBS_dist_Geo_log, dpi = 300)

```

Calculate some stats
```{r}
# Calculate the standard deviation of the distances
sd_distances <- sd(env_distances_matrix)

# Calculate the mean of the distances
mean_distances <- mean(env_distances_matrix)

# Function to calculate confidence interval
confidence_interval <- function(data, confidence = 0.95) {
  n <- length(data)
  se <- sd(data) / sqrt(n)
  alpha <- 1 - confidence
  error_margin <- qt(1 - alpha / 2, df = n - 1) * se
  lower_bound <- mean(data) - error_margin
  upper_bound <- mean(data) + error_margin
  return(c(lower_bound, upper_bound))
}

# Flatten the distance matrix to a vector for CI calculation
distance_vector <- as.vector(env_distances_matrix)

# Calculate the 95% confidence interval for the distances
ci_distances <- confidence_interval(distance_vector)

# Output the results
list(
  max_distance = max(env_distances_matrix),
  mean_distance = mean_distances,
  min_distance = min(env_distances_matrix),
  sd_distance = sd_distances,
  ci_lower_bound = ci_distances[1],
  ci_upper_bound = ci_distances[2]
)
```

```{r}
# Function to create a high-resolution map overlay
create_high_res_map <- function(projection) {
  map_world <- getMap(resolution = "high")
  map <- spTransform(map_world, CRS(projection))
  return(map)
}

# Add the map of the world and adjust the plot
high_res_map <- create_high_res_map("+proj=merc +datum=WGS84")

# Adjust the aspect ratio and other settings of the final plot
final_plot <- plots2$mrates02 +
  #scale_fill_gradientn(colours = brewer.pal(11, "RdBu")) +
  geom_polygon(data = polygon_coords, aes(x = long, y = lat), color = "black", fill = NA) + # Add polygon outline
  #geom_point(data = inside_coords, aes(x = long, y = lat), color = "#c861a5", size = 3) + # Add sample locations within polygon
  theme(
    aspect.ratio = 2.5,  # Adjust the aspect ratio here
    plot.margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10, b = 10, l = 10),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.background = element_blank()
  ) +
  coord_fixed(ratio = 2.5)

# Save the adjusted plot, Figure 5C.
ggsave("EEMS_50demes_without_samples.png", final_plot, width = 10, height = 20, dpi = 600)
ggsave("EEMS_50demes_without_samples.pdf", final_plot, width = 10, height = 20)
```
